downloads.title: Our data
downloads.description:
Chile's Millennium Nucleus on the Impacts of China in Latin America and the Caribbean (ICLAC), the Inter-American Dialogue, and our partners are pleased to make our Chinese foreign direct investment data available to researchers and other users of the Repository.

The full dataset —every investment across all countries in a single file— is available for download above. As we add new countries, they will be incorporated into the same dataset.

The file has three data sheets: investments, one row per investment; sites, the coordinates of every mapped site; and case_studies, the associated studies. All three join on the investment identifier.

We welcome you to submit contributions or corrections through the Contact page. We are grateful for your help keeping our data as accurate and up to date as possible.
downloads.format: XLSX format · one row per investment, plus the sites and case study sheets
downloads.annex_description:
Investments recorded in the base that fall outside the full dataset. An investment ends up here for one of two reasons: its documentary evidence falls below the Repository threshold, meaning no independent source confirms the amount or the type of transaction, or the base marks it as excluded.

The reason for each one is given in the cancelled_motivo column of the file, and it is not the same for all of them: there are cancelled projects, announcements that were never carried out, memoranda of understanding that never broke ground, duplicate entries, and cases outside the scope of the Repository. They are published separately, with their reliability score and their sources, so that the record stays complete and traceable.

They are not part of the full dataset, nor of the figures shown in the map and Trends.
downloads.annex_format: XLSX format · same sheets and columns as the full dataset

footer.tagline: Regional Repository of Chinese Investments in Latin America

landing.title: Regional Repository of Chinese Investments in Latin America
landing.body: The Regional Repository, developed in 2024 by the Chile-based Millennium Nucleus on the Impacts of China in Latin America and the Caribbean, the Inter-American Dialogue, and a team of partners and researchers across the hemisphere, attempts a granular and continuously updated account of confirmed Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) in Latin America and the Caribbean—since China began “going-out” in earnest in the early 2000s. Drawing on the unmatched expertise of on-the-ground partner institutions, this tool provides up-to-date, georeferenced, and downloadable data on Chinese FDI in select countries across the region. In addition to FDI data, the Regional Repository also contains high-quality academic and multilingual case studies on individual Chinese FDI projects. The Regional Repository will be expanded over time to include data on Chinese investment in additional Latin American and Caribbean nations.

map.title: About the map
map.body:
This map, produced by Chile’s Millennium Nucleus on the Impacts of China in Latin America and the Caribbean (ICLAC) and the Inter-American Dialogue, with critical input from partner organizations from across the region, visualizes the extent of Chinese foreign direct investment (mergers and acquisitions, greenfield projects, and joint ventures). It also includes examples of Chinese construction projects, which are prominent in certain economic sectors across the region. The map tool is searchable by year, type of investment, and based on whether these projects have associated case studies. Available studies are accessible in each country’s list of Chinese investments. At present, this project includes analysis of Chinese investment in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname and Uruguay, and estimates of investments in Venezuela, but will soon expand to include projects in several other countries, in coordination with partner institutions.
On the map, points are single-site investments (mines, plants, offices) and vectors mark projects spanning several cities (roads, railways, cables). The book icon means the investment has an academic case study.

trends.title: Regional Trends
trends.body:
In the diagram we show Chinese investments by company, country and sector. The figure can be used to detect regional trends or to identify country-specific tendencies. The width of the lines represents the metric chosen above: number of projects or amount invested. The thickest lines pertain to those Chinese companies that have invested in the most projects in represented countries and to those sectors that have the highest percentage of associated projects.
Each company appears once: subsidiaries are counted under their parent and variants of the same name are merged. The 20 largest are shown; the rest roll up into “Others”. Click any node to filter by it; country, sector and year filters are shared with the map.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.description:
The Regional Repository of Chinese Investments in Latin America represents a collective endeavor to map Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) and construction projects in the Latin American region between 2003 and 2026, and to classify these investments by project type, economic sector, and companies involved. At present, the Repository contains data for Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Jamaica, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, and estimates of investments in Venezuela.


How was the Repository developed?


The production of this Repository is a collaborative endeavor, involving researchers and research institutions from across the Americas. Our team is composed of researchers with wide-ranging, interdisciplinary backgrounds, including political scientists, economists, and geographers. Our work is also made possible by the dedicated participation of numerous research assistants and undergraduate and graduate student researchers from the many universities and research centers affiliated with this project. We are grateful for the contributions of Benjamín Zúñiga Silva, Benjamín Muñoz, Florencia Muñoz, Gonzalo Concha, Catalina Leiva, Felipe Soto, and Allison Stronach from the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile; Eugenio Sánchez from Sciences Po; Claire Espinosa from Princeton University; Yifang Wang, Xinyi Wang, Jessie Hu, Bea Gerard, Kaiyen Fumo-Pegues, Jerry Zhang, and Jessica Shao from the Inter-American Dialogue; and Camilo DeFelipe from the Pontificia Universidad Javeriana. Additionally, we acknowledge the extensive contributions to our research from Juliana González Jauregui in Argentina, Ignacio Tornero in Chile, Cynthia Sanborn and Darissa Cama in Peru, and Juan José Gómez-Aguirre in Colombia. Florencia Muñoz coordinates the team, and Felipe Soto is responsible for the data architecture and the design of the platform. We were fortunate to partner closely with the Center for Studies on China and Asia-Pacific (CECHAP) at the Universidad del Pacífico; the Universidad del Rosario and the Colombia-China Chamber of Commerce; and the China-Argentina Center at the Faculty of Social Sciences of the University of Buenos Aires together with the Argentina-China Chamber of Commerce, when compiling data on Peru, Colombia, and Argentina, respectively. We aim to expand to incorporate more countries in close collaboration with other regional partners.


The Repository was produced by assembling data from ICLAC and partner data sets on Chinese foreign direct investments (FDI) in specific Latin American countries, according to the OECD definition of FDI, which assumes a long-term relationship between the direct investor and the direct investment company or asset and a significant degree of influence (at least 10 percent ownership) over the management of the company. Under “construction” we have also included projects that have been built by Chinese companies but wherein the companies retain no ownership. We analyzed each project using primary and secondary sources to confirm the amount, purpose, location (including geocoordinates), and local partners for each investment in our data set. Our methodology for project selection concluded with an extensive peer review process involving in-country partners and other experts.


Since 2025, the verification process has additionally incorporated language models as a supporting tool, used for three narrowly defined tasks: proposing investments missing from the Repository, cross-checking existing records against new sources, and detecting internal inconsistencies in the dataset. One rule governs the entire procedure: the model proposes, it never confirms. No output enters the Repository without a researcher verifying it against the primary source, and the model is not cited as a source. The full procedure is described in Step 7 of the methodology document.


What does the Repository include?


Our map visualizes China’s investments using both points and vectors, to better represent each project’s geographical ambit. We have used points for investments in assets, such as mines, real estate, or agricultural sites, that don’t traverse multiple cities. Vectors are utilized for roads, rail, cables, and oil blocks. A third case is multi-point investments: projects carried out across several localities without forming a continuous route, such as a portfolio of wind farms or a programme deployed across different municipalities, which are represented with one point per identified site. All aim to provide an accurate representation of the extent of Chinese engagement on a country-by-country and sectoral basis. There is one instance in Chile in which a Chinese company, Tianqi Lithium, acquired a minority stake in a local conglomerate—SQM—which owns many, varied assets across the country. In this instance, we have not visualized all of SQM’s assets in the Repository, but rather those related to lithium, which were the primary motivation for Tianqi Lithium’s acquisition. This is an effort to avoid visually overrepresenting Tianqi Lithium’s 23.77 percent participation in SQM. In each instance, we have aimed to achieve a balance between precision and clarity in the visualization.


The map offers a relatively simplified representation of project locations. However, by downloading the data, users can determine the city or locality where Chinese investments are located, along with other details about each transaction. Our data is accessible in a CSV format by clicking on the Download Data tab at the top of the page.


Each investment in the Repository carries a reliability score from 0 to 5, indicating how many reliable, independent sources support the record. The score equals the number of those sources plus one: a 5 corresponds to four or more primary sources —government documentation, official registries, the company’s own communications, or international reference press— and a 2 to a single reliable source. Investments with a score of 2 or below are not published on the map. The score is available in the downloadable data, together with a note explaining in each case which sources were considered independent and which aspects of the record remain uncorroborated.


We have additionally incorporated high-quality, peer-reviewed case study analysis of these projects, when available, to assist researchers as they pursue new avenues of inquiry or fill critical research gaps. This includes analysis from peer-reviewed journal articles, doctoral dissertations, think tank reports, or government documents that thoroughly examine one or more investments in the Repository. Featured studies contain at least one page of analysis on the China-related project or investor and were published since China invested in or financed the project in question. As users will observe, the research gaps on Chinese investment in these countries are substantial: only about a third of the projects have affiliated case studies, which we indicate with a book icon.


In the case of Venezuela, we have sought to present as accurate a representation as possible of operational Chinese investment, but in general, data on Chinese investment in Venezuela should be interpreted with caution. Official statistics from both Chinese and Venezuelan sources are frequently incomplete, inconsistently reported, or affected by political and institutional opacity. Many projects are financed through complex oil-for-loan arrangements, credit lines, or state enterprise contracts that lack public disclosure, while others are announced but never fully implemented. Independent datasets likewise face gaps due to limited on-the-ground verification and irregular reporting cycles.


The Repository includes greenfield investments, mergers and acquisitions, and joint ventures, all of which feature in our data and are classified accordingly. The map is also limited to projects that are currently operational. Projects that have been announced but for which there is no financing, or sign of “lasting interest” or “significant degree of influence,” are not published. Numerous projects that have been covered extensively in the media do not appear on the map because no progress is evident to date, or else finance has yet to materialize. At the same time, if mining concessions are purchased but remain undeveloped, we have included these deals in the dataset, because they reflect “lasting interest” in mining assets, unless the concession has expired or is suspended. When projects contain both the acquisition of an initial asset and then greenfield investment in that same asset (e.g., an expansion of an existing dam), these projects are classified separately as acquisitions and greenfield, counting the value of each of these transactions. The year recorded for each project corresponds to the commencement of construction work or, in the case of acquisitions, to the year in which the operation was completed.


Projects that do not meet the publication criteria are not discarded: they are kept in an annex of excluded projects, where each record retains all of its fields and additionally carries the reason for exclusion. The annex gathers projects with insufficient evidence, those that were cancelled or suspended, announcements and memoranda of understanding that were never executed, and assets that ceased to be Chinese-owned because they were sold to another company. The amounts in the annex are not added to any aggregate figure of the Repository.


There are cases in which a non-Chinese multinational with assets in Latin America is acquired by a Chinese company. In such cases, from the date of acquisition, the Latin American assets of the acquired company are recorded as Chinese investment, as is any subsequent transaction carried out by the now Chinese-owned entity. COFCO’s acquisition of Nidera’s Latin American holdings is an example of this, and COFCO’s ownership of these assets is reflected in the Repository. Because it is frequently difficult to isolate the precise value of Latin American assets within large global acquisitions, an estimated figure is used when no reliable asset-specific information is available.


All of the projects in the Repository are classified by industry. For our purposes, the Infrastructure classification comprises all transport and facilities-related (e.g., hospitals) investments, including turnkey construction projects. Energy investments include oil and gas, hydroelectricity projects, and renewable energy investments. ICT investments comprise telecommunications, data centres, network equipment, and digital services. Investments in banking or insurance are classified as Finance, but the purchases of office space by Chinese banks that are establishing themselves in the region are labeled as Real Estate transactions. The same is true of other warehouse or office purchases, including by Chinese tech conglomerates. Agribusiness incorporates any agricultural investments, including food-related deals and agrochemical investments. Our Manufacturing category mainly includes machinery, car, bus, auto parts, and electrical equipment manufacturing. The projects categorized as Mining each include the acquisition or development of mining sites, but also any possible related investment in mining equipment, investments related to site preparation, site-specific infrastructure, exploration, and other related activities.


In addition to foreign direct investment, the Repository also attempts to capture instances of Chinese construction, often through public works contracts, which have historically been an important feature of Chinese infrastructure engagement with the Latin American region. In these cases, Chinese companies retain no ownership of these assets. Their obligations cease once construction is finished.


Can Repository users contribute information on Chinese investments in Latin America?


As noted, all Repository data is the product of a rigorous research process that has included the triangulation of primary and secondary data sources, as well as consultations with experts to verify the details of documented transactions. However, we are aware that the landscape of FDI in the region is continually evolving. We appreciate your collaboration in keeping our data as accurate and up to date as possible. We invite users to contribute to and edit our data via the “Contact Us” tab located at the top of our page.


The Repository is made possible with funding from Chile’s Núcleo Milenio program, which promotes collaborative research in support of Chile’s development, from the National Agency for Research and Development (ANID, grants 11180081 and 1230307), and by the Henry Luce Foundation. We hope that the data will be used to advance academic research and other analysis.

filter.title: Filters
filter.type_off_only: Not applicable while showing construction only.
filter.construction_help:
Construction projects are public works contracts wherein Chinese companies engage in the design, sourcing of materials, and/or physical building of projects, but do not retain equity in or ownership of the project. These projects do not qualify as FDI by the OECD definition, but are included in our data to demonstrate the full scale of China's involvement in regional infrastructure development.
Construction projects are excluded from the map by default. Choose “With construction projects” to add them to the figures above, or “Only construction projects” to see them on their own.
